intro: You have a dispute that looks like it may end up in court, and you want a civil litigation solicitor you can actually get to. Searching for a civil litigation solicitor near me usually means you want someone local enough to meet, who understands the court you would be dealing with and can take the matter from a letter before action through to trial and enforcement if needed.
need_heading: What people searching for a civil litigation solicitor near me usually need
need_lead: Most people behind this search are weighing up a real dispute and want to know where they stand before it escalates.
needs: You have sent or received a letter before action and need to know what happens next and by when.
A business or individual owes you money and you are considering issuing a claim to recover it.
You have been served with court papers and need help responding within the time the court has set.
A contract or building dispute has stalled and you want advice on whether to settle or press on.
You are unsure whether your claim is still in time, because limitation periods apply to civil claims.
context_heading: Checking who can handle your litigation
context: The word lawyer is not protected on its own, so it is worth confirming that the person handling your matter is a solicitor, a chartered legal executive or another authorised professional. Reserved activities such as conducting court litigation can only be carried out by authorised people. Solicitors in England and Wales are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority, and you can check an individual or firm on the SRA register; in Scotland it is the Law Society of Scotland, and in Northern Ireland the Law Society of Northern Ireland.

Regulated firms must hold professional indemnity insurance and have a complaints procedure. If a service complaint is not resolved that way, the Legal Ombudsman can look at it in England and Wales. Because searching near me often reflects a wish to meet in person or deal with your local court, ask the solicitor which courts they cover and how they would handle hearings that fall elsewhere.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the dispute in plain terms, including what it is about and who the other side is.
Say whether a letter before action has been sent or received, and when.
Mention any court papers you have been served with and the date on them.
Explain what outcome you are hoping for, such as payment, an apology or the dispute ending.
Say where you are based and which court or area the matter relates to, since you searched near me.
Ask about funding options, including whether a fixed fee or hourly rate is likely.
questions_heading: Questions to ask the civil litigation solicitor
questions: Are you authorised to conduct court litigation, and where can I check your regulation?
Is my claim still within the limitation period that applies to it?
What are the costs consequences if I make or refuse a settlement offer?
How would you fund this matter, and what funding options are open to me?
Which courts would handle this, and would you attend hearings in person?
What do you need from me first, and what happens if we cannot settle before trial?

faqs.q: What does a civil litigation solicitor actually do?
faqs.a: Civil litigation solicitors take disputes through court, from letters before action to trial and enforcement. They can also advise on settling before a hearing, which is often quicker and less costly than going all the way.

faqs.q: How do I check that someone is a solicitor?
faqs.a: In England and Wales you can check an individual or firm on the Solicitors Regulation Authority register. In Scotland check with the Law Society of Scotland, and in Northern Ireland with the Law Society of Northern Ireland.

faqs.q: Why does limitation matter in my dispute?
faqs.a: Limitation periods apply to civil claims, and if one expires you may lose the right to bring the claim at all. Tell the solicitor when the dispute arose so they can advise on timing.

faqs.q: What should I ask about funding?
faqs.a: Ask about funding options early, because civil litigation can be paid for in different ways. Also ask what the costs consequences would be if you make or refuse a settlement offer.
